parsed.canonical_question: Why does anaerobic respiration produce far less ATP than aerobic respiration?

render.title: Anaerobic respiration versus aerobic
render.body:
When a cell runs out of oxygen, its ATP production falls sharply from about 30 down to just 2 per glucose. Here is why.

Aerobic respiration has three stages: glycolysis in the cytoplasm, the Krebs cycle in the mitochondrial matrix, and oxidative phosphorylation on the inner mitochondrial membrane. The first two stages produce a large number of electron carriers, mainly NADH and FADH2. These carriers feed electrons into the electron transport chain, which uses their energy to pump protons across the inner membrane, building up a proton gradient. That gradient drives ATP synthase to produce roughly 26-28 ATP. Glycolysis and the Krebs cycle together add about 4 more, giving a total of around 30-32 ATP per glucose.

Oxygen is essential as the final electron acceptor at Complex IV. It receives the electrons at the end of the chain and combines with protons to form water. Without oxygen, electrons have nowhere to go. The entire electron transport chain grinds to a halt, the proton gradient collapses, and ATP synthase stops spinning.

Without the electron transport chain, the cell cannot regenerate NAD+ from NADH in the normal way. NAD+ is needed to keep glycolysis and the Krebs cycle running. To survive, the cell switches to fermentation (for example, lactic acid fermentation in human muscle cells), which regenerates NAD+ without using oxygen. This allows glycolysis to continue, but glycolysis alone produces only 2 ATP per glucose through substrate-level phosphorylation. The Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation are both off.

In short: about 28 of the roughly 30 ATP come from the electron transport chain and ATP synthase, which both require oxygen. Remove oxygen and you lose that entire contribution, leaving only the 2 ATP from glycolysis.
render.summary: Without oxygen, the electron transport chain stops because it has no final electron acceptor. This collapses the proton gradient, silencing ATP synthase. The cell falls back on glycolysis alone, which yields only 2 ATP per glucose by substrate-level phosphorylation instead of the roughly 30 that aerobic respiration provides.
